it is useful to describe basic nomenclature for needle and probe manipulation.
Much of this is derived from the American Institute of Ultrasound in Medicine Standards.

Long axis imaging is of limited use in ultrasound guided peripheral nerve blocks.
An ultrasound transducer can be rotated or translated.
along any of its three axes, and we need to use the AIUM standards so that we can communicate clearly with one another.
Here we see an ultrasound probe moving and pivoting along each of its X, Y, and Z axes.
Each of these movements has a...
name that we will define in the next section.
Sliding is a min-
maneuver that translates the transducer along the course of its structure or perpendicular
to it to scan adjacent structures.
Impression is a useful...
over that has numerous effects. First, it moves the active face toward deeper structures
to make them appear more superficial.
It also helps differentiate between different structures
by their relative compressibility.
Vains are easy to compress, arteries are somewhat compressed.
and pulsatile, and nerves are fairly incompressible.
Rocking allows us to...
extend the plane of imaging when we are working in a narrow acoustic window.
Rotation is used to switch between short axis and long axis imaging.
Hilting allows us to scan along the course of a structure through a narrow acoustic window.

Block needles are specular reflect-
factors, meaning they reflect sound back to the receiver over a narrow angle.
As the angle between the transducer and needle increases, less sound.
is reflected back to the receiver, and the signal becomes weaker.
We can also see that this is true for sound reflected off the sides of the needle.
shaft. With the short axis out of plane approach, the needle will be seen best when the tip is within the plane of imaging.
The shaft gives a signal that may be no stronger than surrounding structures.
Generally, tissue displacement...
is transmitted far enough along tissue planes for the operator to get a sense for the trajectory
of the needle. This is a dynamic process, and we're live-
on the operator's ability to detect tissue displacement created by needle movement.
Staccato movement should be avoided.
Needle position can also be inferred by observing the distribution of small test injections
and making needle adjustments.
Often, slight tilting of the probe can be used to locate and follow the advancing needle tip.
In plain needle manipulation offers its own set of challenges.

The needle is much
better resolved when it is inserted at a shallow angle relative to the transducer.
The next set of problems occurs when the needle trajectory
straights from the plane of imaging. If the needle crosses the plane of imaging, but does not completely lie within it, only a portion of the
needle will be seen. This can give a false impression of needle depth that can lead to complications.
Alignment issues can often be addressed by leaving the needle stationary and manipulating
the transducer until the tip of the needle is imaged.
The needle-
level has a characteristic stair step appearance that should be sought out.
